sentences: What a mind run on far more neurons could still count as a mind is the question just opened.
That brains and neural nets share one bounded design is now settled; what scaling it up buys is still open.
That design explains why language is discrete and single-threaded; bigger brains would only shift its balance, not replace it.
Extending that design to sensing and acting, bigger brains would catch more hidden order, not escape it.
Within that frame, abstraction appears as a climbable network of hidden order, its reach for bigger brains still unmeasured.
Computational language offers the clearest test yet, reaching real meta-level thought ordinary language can't, but hitting the same wall.
Since one brain holds only one thread, more complex coordination among many threads is what bigger brains could add to society.
The scaling story resolves here: a bigger brain simply claims more of the space of all computation, still recognizably a mind.
Whether AI can truly feel is still unsettled, yet moral stakes for both machines and humans already follow from the answer.
Before any evidence is weighed, psychological bias alone explains much of the pull toward seeing machines as conscious.
Bias cleared away, the deeper question is technical: does computation itself suffice for experience, and four lines of argument say likely not.
If machine consciousness stays genuinely uncertain, caution about creating it matters as much as judging whether it already exists.
Neither proved nor disproved, machine consciousness still leaves the more urgent task of not mistaking our own minds for its algorithms.
GPT-3 merely scales an old design, yet learns to learn; why that works is still unexplained.
Scaling already works for GPT-3; now the claim widens to intelligence itself as a product of scale.
An ensemble story explains why scale works; a loss-based theory backs it, but what more scale buys stays unknown.
Granting scaling's power, what's unsettled is who will actually commit resources to pushing it further.
Looking back, scaling's skeptics were repeatedly wrong, while dismissals of 'mere' mechanism miss what success must look like.
Scaling's promise now carries a cost: models trained on human data may inherit real agency.
Even stripped of human content, abstract systems still admit agent-like behavior, hard to rule out anywhere.
The case made, what remains is only pointers to sources and related pages.
A corroded lump pulled from the sea would take decades to be read as a machine, and still resists a firm birthdate.
Known only through broken pieces, the puzzle is what fraction of its original design they actually preserve.
Even its visible face hides a dispute over a basic fact, how many days its calendar ring counted.
With the day-count still unsettled, attention turns to what the dial's pointers and inscriptions tracked in the sky.
Having modelled Sun and Moon on its face, the back is shown tracking still longer calendar and eclipse cycles.
All this is secure, but one spare gear reopens the question of a display never found: the planets.
Explaining the planets means guessing gears that no longer exist, and every guess so far falls short of the evidence.
The device looks unique only until Roman and later Eastern accounts of kindred machines are counted.
What remains unresolved in the gears is settled instead in replicas, screens, and stories built around the mechanism.
What tells real science from empty imitation is still unnamed, and that is the stake here.
Many popular beliefs fail the plainest test of working; why they still pass for science is unexplained.
Cargo Cult Science names form without result, and integrity is proposed as the missing ingredient.
Integrity against self-deception is defined; still open is how far it must extend to the public and policy.
Cases from psychology, physics, and ESP confirm the diagnosis, closing on a wish for the freedom to keep it.
